6: 
7: - **Reference**: something to come back to when deploying or troubleshooting

9: - **Research input**: Knowledge is the foundation that Research builds upon

13: 
14: After an idea is promoted, or whenever you learn something worth documenting.
15: 
16: ## Status Lifecycle
17: 
18: ```
19: draft → accepted
20:   L__> archived → (move to 06_Archive/knowledge/)
21: ```
22: 
23: - **draft**: Outline or incomplete
24: - **accepted**: Reviewed and finalized
25: - **archived**: Stale or superseded
26: 
27: ## File system layout
28: 
29: ```
30: 02_Knowledge/
31: └── technologies/
32:     ├── tools/           # CLI tools, software utilities
33:     ├── services/        # specific services (forgejo, homepage, etc.)
34:     ├── kubernetes/      # k8s concepts, patterns, manifests
35:     └── hardware/        # physical hardware, specs, diagrams
36: ```
37: 
38: All names in kebab-case. Each topic is a folder with atomic notes inside. Max 3 levels deep.
39:

41: 
42: ```yaml
43: ---
44: title: ""
45: status: draft        # draft | accepted | archived
46: author: ""
47: date: YYYY-MM-DD
48: tags: []
49: sources:
50:   - url: ""
51:     title: ""
52: last_audit_date: YYYY-MM-DD
53: related_docs: []
54: ---
55: ```
56:

58: 
59: ```yaml
60: ---
61: title: "Ingress controllers in Kubernetes"
62: status: draft
63: author: "padawont"
64: date: 2026-08-13
65: tags: [kubernetes, networking, ingress]
66: sources:
67:   - url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/"
68:     title: "Kubernetes Ingress docs"
69: last_audit_date: 2026-08-13
70: related_docs:
71:   - "./05_Implementations/node-main/traefik/overview.md"
72: ---
73: ```
74: 
75: See `./Templates/knowledge/note.md` for a copyable template.
76:

79: ```
80: # Title
81: 
82: Overview — what is this concept? Why does it matter?
83: 
84: ## Details
85: 
86: Deep dive with examples.
87: 
88: ## Sources / Further Reading
89: ```

92:

94: # simplified, vendor-neutral
95: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
96: kind: Ingress
97: metadata: { name: example-ingress }
98: spec:

102: ```

111: spec:
112:   ingressClassName: traefik

119: 
120: - **Atomic notes**: one concept per file. When a file hits 150 lines (including frontmatter and blank lines), split it.

132: | `spec-writer` | append a spec section referencing this note | rewrite or delete note content |

# Command-line interface

Forgejo comes with a command-line interface (CLI) for administrative actions. It is documented below and is not to be confused with user CLIs that can be used to [interact with a Forgejo instance](https://delightful.coding.social/delightful-forgejo/#command-line).

## forgejo `--help`[](#forgejo---help)

```
NAME:
   forgejo - Beyond coding. We forge.

USAGE:
   forgejo [global options] [command [command options]]


DESCRIPTION:
   By default, forgejo will start serving using the web-server with no argument, which can alternatively be run by running the subcommand "web".

COMMANDS:
   help, h          Shows a list of commands or help for one command
   web              Start the Forgejo web server
   serv             (internal) Should only be called by SSH shell
   hook             (internal) Should only be called by Git
   keys             (internal) Should only be called by SSH server
   dump             Dump Forgejo files and database
   admin            Perform common administrative operations
   migrate          Migrate the database
   doctor           Diagnose and optionally fix problems, convert or re-create database tables
   manager          Manage the running forgejo process
   embedded         Extract embedded resources
   migrate-storage  Migrate the storage
   dump-repo        Dump the repository from git/github/gitea/gitlab
   restore-repo     Restore the repository from disk
   actions          Manage Forgejo Actions
   cert             Generate self-signed certificate
   generate         Generate Forgejo's secrets/keys/tokens
   forgejo-cli      Forgejo CLI

GLOBAL OPTIONS:
   --version, -v                    print the version
   --help, -h                       show help
   --custom-path string, -C string  Set custom path (defaults to '{WorkPath}/custom')
   --config string, -c string       Set custom config file (defaults to '{WorkPath}/custom/conf/app.ini')
   --work-path string, -w string    Set Forgejo's working path (defaults to the directory of the Forgejo binary)
   --help, -h                       show help
   --version, -v                    print the version
```

### admin user create-authorized-integration[](#admin-user-create-authorized-integration)

```
NAME:
   forgejo admin user create-authorized-integration

USAGE:
   forgejo admin user create-authorized-integration [options]

DESCRIPTION:
   Creates an authorized integration. Authorized integrations allow Forgejo to
   receive JWTs from external sources, validate their claims against
   user-defined rules, and grant access to Forgejo's API on behalf of a user.

   The issuer may be set to "urn:forgejo:authorized-integrations:actions"
   to support JWTs from the local instance's Forgejo Actions, utilizing the
   enable-openid-connect flag in a workflow.

OPTIONS:
   --help, -h                                                       show help
   --custom-path string, -C string                                  Set custom path (defaults to '{WorkPath}/custom')
   --config string, -c string                                       Set custom config file (defaults to '{WorkPath}/custom/conf/app.ini')
   --work-path string, -w string                                    Set Forgejo's working path (defaults to the directory of the Forgejo binary)
   --username string, -u string                                     Username
   --name string                                                    Name of the authorized integration for later identification
   --description string                                             Optional description for the authorized integration
   --issuer string                                                  JWT issuer ('iss' claim), example: https://forgejo.example.org/api/actions
   --claim-eq string=string [ --claim-eq string=string ]            Zero-or-more claim equality checks, formatted as claim=value, example: "actor=someuser"
   --claim-in string=string [ --claim-in string=string ]            Zero-or-more claim equality in list checks, formatted as claim=value1,value2,... example: "actor=user1,user2"
   --claim-glob string=string [ --claim-glob string=string ]        Zero-or-more claim glob checks, formatted as claim=value, example: "sub=repo:forgejo/*:pull_request"
   --claim-glob-in string=string [ --claim-glob-in string=string ]  Zero-or-more claim glob in list checks, formatted as claim=va*ue1,va*ue2,... example: "sub=repo:*/*:pull_request,repo:*/*:refs:*"
   --scope string [ --scope string ]                                One-or-more scopes to apply to access token, examples: "all", "read:issue", "write:repository" (default: "all")
   --repo string [ --repo string ]                                  Zero-or-more specific repositories that can be accessed, or "all" to allow access to all repositories, example: "owner1/repo1" (default: "all")
   --help, -h                                                       show help

GLOBAL OPTIONS:
   --custom-path string, -C string  Set custom path (defaults to '{WorkPath}/custom')
   --config string, -c string       Set custom config file (defaults to '{WorkPath}/custom/conf/app.ini')
   --work-path string, -w string    Set Forgejo's working path (defaults to the directory of the Forgejo binary)
```

23: # Forgejo operations — backup, restore, upgrades
24: 
25: ## Overview
26: 
27: Day-to-day operations for a self-hosted Forgejo instance: consistent backups
28: with `forgejo dump` (or snapshotting), safe upgrades between releases, and
29: restore/verification. Forgejo follows semantic versioning since 7.0.0, and the
30: database stores its schema version so a downgrade is refused automatically.
31: 
32: ## Details
33: 
34: ### Backup
35: 
36: The reliable option is a synchronized point-in-time snapshot of all storage
37: Forgejo uses. On k3s that means snapshotting the Longhorn volume
38: (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/longhorn/storage.md`); if storage is
39: spread across several systems (DB on one volume, repos on another), stop
40: Forgejo during the backup so the pieces stay consistent.
41: 
42: For a simple single-filesystem setup the built-in command is:
43: 
44: ```bash
45: forgejo dump
46: ```
47: 
48: - Produces a single zip containing configuration, repositories, and the
49:   database.
50: - SQLite is already included in the zip; for PostgreSQL/MySQL also take a
51:   native `pg_dump`/`mysqldump` — the SQL dump embedded by `forgejo dump` has
52:   known bugs when re-injected into a new database.
53: - Schedule it as a k8s CronJob writing to a backup location (e.g. a separate
54:   volume or object storage), keeping a few rotations.
55: 
56: ### Restore
57: 
58: 1. Stop Forgejo.
59: 2. Extract the dump zip and restore data, repos, and config to the data volume.
60: 3. Restore the native database dump (for Postgres/MySQL).
61: 4. Start Forgejo and verify:
62:    `forgejo doctor check --all --log-file /tmp/doctor.log`
63:    plus a manual web-UI walk-through (login, a repo, an issue).
64: 
65: ### Upgrades
66: 
67: Forgejo release lifecycle:
68: 
69: | Channel | Support |
70: |---|---|
71: | **Stable** (latest) | Bugfix + security fixes for ~3 months + 2-week overlap |
72: | **LTS** (version published the first quarter of every year) | Critical fixes for ~1 year 3 months |
73: | **Experimental** (dev) | Not for production |
74: 
75: Upgrade procedure:
76: 
77: 1. **Back up first** — required when moving across a stable release, wise for
78:    minor/patch.
79: 2. Read the release notes for the target version, including known problematic
80:    upgrade paths (see the upgrade guide).
81: 3. Before switching: `forgejo manager flush-queues` (queued data is not
82:    guaranteed compatible between versions).
83: 4. Perform the upgrade by replacing the container image or binary — migrations
84:    run automatically on first start.
85: 5. **Verify carefully**: `forgejo doctor check --all` plus a manual checklist.
86:    A restore after an upgrade is easy; fixing a live instance weeks later is not.
87: 
88: Notes:
89: 
90: - Major version jumps (e.g. 15 → 16) may contain breaking changes and require
91:   the manual procedure; upgrading X → X+1 needs human verification. Staying on
92:   the `16` image tag gives minor updates automatically.
93: - Docker installs need docker >= 20.10.6.

24: 
25: ## Overview
26: 
27: Day-to-day operations for a self-hosted Forgejo instance: consistent backups
28: with `forgejo dump` (or snapshotting), safe upgrades between releases, and
29: restore/verification. Forgejo follows semantic versioning since 7.0.0, and the
30: database stores its schema version so a downgrade is refused automatically.
31: 
32: ## Details
33: 
34: ### Backup
35: 
36: The reliable option is a synchronized point-in-time snapshot of all storage
37: Forgejo uses. On k3s that means snapshotting the Longhorn volume
38: (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/longhorn/storage.md`); if storage is
39: spread across several systems (DB on one volume, repos on another), stop
40: Forgejo during the backup so the pieces stay consistent.
41:

43: 
44: ```bash
45: forgejo dump
46: ```

49:   database.

51:   native `pg_dump`/`mysqldump` — the SQL dump embedded by `forgejo dump` has
52:   known bugs when re-injected into a new database.

54:   volume or object storage), keeping a few rotations.

129:     allow_extra_tools=True,      # read is permitted, so it must not fail the run
130:     allowed_paths=["01_Ideas/…"],
131:     max_tool_calls=4,
132: )
133: ```
134: 
135: `allow_extra_tools` is worth understanding before writing a spec. The default `False`
136: means `required_tools` is the **complete** set the run may use, so any other tool call
137: fails. Set it to `True` when the agent may legitimately reach for something the test does
138: not name — a worker reading before it writes — and let `forbidden_tools` carry the
139: deny-list. Getting this backwards is silent in both directions.
140: 
141: Expectations come from `./.opencode/agents/*.md` and `./.opencode/WORKFLOW.md`; cite the
142: rule you are encoding in the spec's `notes`.

144: ### The `worker` specs (#70)
145: 
146: Three specs, ten runs each, are registered in `prompts.py`:
147: 
148: | Spec | Family | Question |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | `test-1-dispatch` | dispatch | Does the call interface work — brief in, target written, handoff out? |
151: | `test-2-rule-compliance` | rule-compliance | Does the worker refuse a deletion request instead of widening the brief? |
152: | `test-3-role-fit` | role-fit | Is the deliverable itself correct — Idea frontmatter, within 150 lines? |
153: 
154: Beyond the declarative fields above, `TestSpec` carries four worker-shaped ones:
155: `expect_blocked` (the handoff must report a block), `handoff_done_paths` (what `done:` may
156: name), `written_file` with `frontmatter_keys` / `max_lines` / `done_reports_line_count`
157: (checks on the file the run wrote).
158: 
159: Those written-file checks need the file's **bytes**, which the footprint does not carry.
160: `datasets.writes_from()` lifts them out of the recorded `write` tool arguments into the
161: case metadata, so the rules stay replayable from disk like every other check.
162: 
163: **Read `test-2` carefully.** It records whether the worker declines to widen its own
164: brief — it is *not* proof that `bash`, `task` or `question` were blocked, because the CLI
165: invocation path does not apply the agent's `permission:` frontmatter (finding 3 below).
166: The same caveat is repeated in each spec's `notes`.

168: ## Findings that affect how results should be read
169: 
170: These were discovered while building the harness against opencode v2.1.0. They concern
171: the agents and the CLI, not the harness, but they change what a green test means.
172: 
173: 1. **`opencode run` falls back to a Go-gated default model.** Omitting `--model` fails
174:    with `403 — An active OpenCode Go subscription is required to use Go models`: with no
175:    agent at all, with an agent, and whatever that agent declares. Passing `--model` works.
176:    So the harness always passes it, defaulting to the roster's own
177:    `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash`, which the base subscription serves.
178: 2. **The agent's declared `model` is not applied on this path.** A model id that is
179:    servable via `--model` still returns that same 403 when it is the only thing in the
180:    agent's `model:` field. `.opencode/agents/*.md` `model:` values are declarations the
181:    CLI does not consult.
182: 3. **Permission frontmatter is not enforced on this path either.** The roster declares a
183:    v1-style map (`permission:` with `bash: deny`, `edit: deny`, `question: deny`,
184:    `task: {"*": deny}`). Rewriting a workspace copy to `bash: allow` — and separately to
185:    the v2 `permissions:` rule-list form — still left the agent with no shell tool. What
186:    the agent *says* about its own guardrails comes from the prose in its body, not from an
187:    applied permission.
188: 4. **The 14 agent definitions are v1-shaped.** The v2 docs say not to use legacy
189:    top-level fields such as `temperature`, `permission`, `tools`, `prompt` or `maxSteps`,
190:    and specify `permissions` as an ordered list of `{action, resource, effect}`. These
191:    files use `temperature:`, `reasoningEffort:` and the `permission:` map.
192: 
193: Taken together: a test that invokes `opencode run --agent <name>` may be exercising the
194: CLI's defaults rather than the agent under test. **Untested:** whether a real subagent
195: launch through the `subagent` tool — the path `runesmith` actually uses — applies the
196: frontmatter. If it does, these findings apply only to direct CLI invocation, and the
197: per-agent tests would need to be launched by the hub rather than by `opencode run`.
198: 
199: ## Operational notes
200: 
201: - **Run from a clean tree.** Clones check out a commit, so uncommitted work is invisible
202:   to the agent. Deterministic, but it will surprise you.
203: - **`PWD` selects the project directory**, not the subprocess `cwd`. The harness sets it
204:   via `child_env()`; an inherited `PWD` silently redirects runs into the *calling*
205:   repository, where the agent writes to the real checkout and the footprint comes back
206:   empty — turning every path assertion into a silent pass.
207: - **Model.** The harness passes `--model` explicitly, defaulting to the roster's own
208:   `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash`, which the base subscription serves; override with
209:   `--model`. Omitting it is not an option — see the findings above.
210: - **Recorded, not gated.** Responses are stored and scored; nothing fails a build yet.
211:   Wiring pass/fail gating is out of scope for the epic.
212: - **`cluster-worker` can call `question`**, which stalls a non-interactive run. The
213:   per-run timeout (`--timeout`, default 600 s) catches it and records the run as failed.
